Rule number 1: everyone is
creative

blocks.html:
• There is nobody in the world who is not creative. Don’t say “my sister is the creative one because she paints.”
  • When you think, parts of your brain light up. Thinking and creativity go together.
  • The only difference is the score. Some people are at 4 out of 10, some at 6, some at 7. This course helps you move up the scale.
blocks.text:
There is nobody in the world who is not creative. Don’t say “my sister is the creative one because she paints.” When you think, parts of your brain light up .
Thinking and creativity go together. The only difference is the score. Some people are
at 4 out of 10 , some at 6, some at 7. This course helps
you move up the scale.

The definition

blocks.html: Creativity is bringing into existence something that did not exist before.

blocks.html: This is the classic definition. Examples:

  • You write a page on a blank sheet.
  • You crumple paper into balls and juggle them.

Why
and when should you be creative? Maslow’s hierarchy of needs

blocks.html: Abraham Maslow said all humans have five levels of needs.
blocks.text:
Abraham Maslow said all humans have five levels of
needs.

blocks.caption:
Five levels of needs, from
basic needs at the bottom to self-actualisation at the top.

blocks.html:
Level Need Examples from the lecture
1 (bottom) Physiological (basic) Food, water, warmth, rest. We take jobs and build houses for these.
2 Safety Locks, a watchman, a government job with a pension
3 Belongingness and love Family, friends, WhatsApp groups. The fear of loneliness is one of our greatest fears. Social media is all about this need.
4 Esteem Prestige and a feeling of accomplishment: a new car, a housewarming, your degree certificate
5 (top) Self-actualisation Reaching your full potential, including creative work and finding meaning. A friend of the professor left everything at 35–40 to start a children’s home.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the “top-end” car trap A car salesman showed the professor the top-end model first (about ₹11.5 lakh). After that, the basic model felt disappointing, even though it cost only about ₹5–6 lakh. This trick is called anchoring: the first number you see sets your expectation. (In the end, he just repaired his old car.)

blocks.html: So why be creative? Because you need creativity to meet every level of need: to earn money for food, to keep your family safe, to make friends and calm an angry parent, to win respect, and to reach your potential.

From problem to solution

blocks.caption:
Creativity starts with a problem and
ends with a solution, and the journey never ends.

blocks.html:
• Creativity starts with a problem and ends with a solution.
  • You find the solution and implement it. Only then can you call yourself creative.
  • It is not a one-time thing. Every day might bring 5 problems and 3 solutions. The journey never ends.
blocks.text:
Creativity starts with a problem and ends
with a solution . You find the solution and
implement it. Only then can you call yourself creative. It is not a one-time thing . Every day might bring 5
problems and 3 solutions. The journey never ends.
What is a problem?

blocks.html: Ask yourself these questions:
blocks.text: Ask yourself these questions:

blocks.html:
Question The professor’s thoughts
What does a problem look like? How does it feel? You can’t touch it, but you feel it: anxious, frustrated, sometimes joyful.
What types of problems are there? Big, small, family, friends, water, buying a car… All of them fit into Maslow’s needs.
Why are some easy and some hard? It depends on the problem, the information you have, and other people. Finding a pencil is easy. Ending poverty is very hard.
How do we usually solve problems? There is no ready answer, but we do solve them, well or badly.
When are you happy solving a problem? He is happy teaching this course, because he wants students to reach the top.
Which problems bore or irritate you? Housework; checking the gas and locks before going out; shuffling two cars in a narrow car park every day.

What is a solution?

blocks.html:
• A solution is the way to solve a problem.
  • Closure means the problem is actually finished. Shuffling the cars is only solved when both cars are back in place.
  • Most everyday solutions are copied from others or come from past experience (“How did I solve this two years ago?”). Copying from nature is called biomimicry.
  • Some problems, like poverty, need extra creative effort.

Way 2: Use empathy

blocks.html: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else’s shoes and looking at the problem from their point of view. It is the easiest way to find problems, because problems belong to people.
blocks.text:
Empathy means putting yourself in someone else’s
shoes and looking at the problem from their point of
view . It is the easiest way to find problems ,
because problems belong to people.

blocks.caption:
Put on the “empathy hat” and you start to
see problems you never noticed.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the empathy walk at IIT Madras Students go on an empathy walk around campus, wearing an imaginary “empathy hat”. At the campus hospital, one student sees a mother and her child in a long queue for the doctor. There are 12 people ahead of them, and the child is getting hungry and cranky. The student imagines being that mother. Now a clear problem appears: “How can parents handle children’s hunger and crankiness while waiting in a queue?” The goal at this stage is only to find the problem, not to solve it yet.

blocks.text:
The 7-step process of
creativity

blocks.caption:
Define, collect, redefine, generate,
design, evaluate, implement.

blocks.html:
Step What you do
1. Define the problem Decide which problem you want to address. Don’t shy away.
2. Collect information Understand the problem fully before you try to solve it.
3. Redefine the problem Use the information to make the problem sharper or more doable.
4. Generate ideas Come up with many ideas to address the redefined problem. Don’t judge them yet.
5. Design the solution Choose an idea (because it is exciting or practical) and shape it into a solution.
6. Evaluate feasibility and refine Check what could go wrong, and fix each issue.
7. Implement the solution Put it into action. Without implementation, there is no creativity.

blocks.html: Skip any step, and you can’t call yourself creative. Creativity is discipline: step by step.

What “redefine” means:
the hunger example

blocks.html:
• Problem: world hunger. It is too big to solve directly.
  • Information: about 100 million children go hungry; malnutrition means people don’t get enough nutrients from their food.
  • Redefined problem: “How can I add nutrients to the food people already eat?” This is a smaller problem that you can actually work on.
blocks.text:
Problem: world hunger. It is too big to solve
directly. Information: about 100 million children go hungry; malnutrition means people don’t get enough nutrients
from their food. Redefined problem: “How can I add
nutrients to the food people already eat?” This is a smaller
problem that you can actually work on.

Full
worked example: “I want my children to learn English”

blocks.html:
Step What the professor did
1. Define “I want my children to learn English.”
2. Collect information They are 15 and 17. They love movies and like English. They have 3 months’ holiday (April–June) and 15 days in December. He is willing to spend some money.
3. Redefine “I want my children to fall in love with English.” This leads to different ideas from just “learn English”.
4. Generate ideas Watch English movies; read books; speak English at home; move to an English-speaking neighbourhood; send them to England.
5. Design He chooses “send them to England for a summer course”.
6. Evaluate and refine No money? Borrow from a bank or friends. Allergic to cold? Go in summer. Nowhere to stay? Call old colleagues living in England.
7. Implement Book the course and the family stay, and put them on the plane.

Imagination
exercises (write in your notebook)

blocks.html:
Exercise The professor’s answer
A paper plane can deliver one message. What would it say, and to whom? To all scientists working on the environment: “Please hurry up with your solutions — we are in grave danger.”
You can become an animal or bird for a day. Which one, and why? A lion, to find out if it really is the king of the jungle.
A statue comes alive. What would you talk about? He would ask the statue of the poet and freedom fighter Subramania Bharathi on the Chennai beach where his inspiration came from, and whether he wrote his poems in one flow.

blocks.html: “Curiosity is the fuel for discovery, inquiry and learning.”
blocks.text: “Curiosity is the fuel for discovery, inquiry and learning.”

blocks.html: Curiosity = seeking information + asking questions. The more questions you ask, the more answers you get.

Four dimensions of curiosity

blocks.caption:
Joyous exploration,
deprivation sensitivity, openness to people’s ideas, stress
tolerance.

blocks.html:
Dimension Meaning Example
Joyous exploration Pleasure from exploring and learning new things Enjoying finding out how trees work
Deprivation sensitivity Noticing a gap in your knowledge and wanting to close it; relief when it closes A thriller that never tells you who the murderer was would drive you mad
Openness to people’s ideas Valuing different views; deliberately asking others for their approach “What is your view on this?”
Stress tolerance Being willing to put up with the discomfort of the new, unfamiliar or uncertain Sitting on the edge of your seat for 2 hours to see the ending (the professor admits he skips to the last episode!)

Tool 4: Intersections

blocks.html: When two ideas meet, a third idea is born. This idea comes from The Medici Effect by Frans Johansson.
blocks.text:
When two ideas meet, a third idea is born. This idea
comes from The Medici Effect by Frans
Johansson .

blocks.html: Lecture example — Peter Café Sport, Horta, Portugal A café on an island where sailors from many countries meet before crossing the Atlantic. One fisherman uses a hook. Another uses bait in a sack cloth, so unwanted fish can be thrown back unhurt. Put the two ideas together, and a new kind of hook that doesn’t hurt the fish may be born.
blocks.text:

blocks.html: Lecture example — the Eastgate Centre, Harare (Zimbabwe) Architect Mick Pearce had to build an office and shopping complex without heavy air conditioning. He had also studied how termites keep their mounds cool: cool air enters at night and warm air leaves. He combined architecture + termite mounds. The building ventilates, cools and heats itself through natural means, saving a lot of energy.

blocks.html: Copying nature to solve human problems like this is called biomimicry.

blocks.html: More examples: pencil + eraser = a pencil with an eraser on top. Camera + water (transparent) = a transparent camera.

How to use intersections

blocks.html:
• Ideas multiply when you break down associative barriers (stop thinking “these two things are unrelated”) and step into the intersection.
  • Learn related-but-unusual subjects. A data science student can borrow ideas from cooking or gardening to solve a data problem.
  • Keep questions in mind so you spot connections by chance (serendipity).
  • Be deliberately creative.

blocks.html: An attitude is a mental frame for looking at something. You might have a great attitude for talking to people but a poor one for hard work. Here is what you need for creativity.
blocks.text:
An attitude is a mental frame for
looking at something. You might have a great attitude for talking to
people but a poor one for hard work. Here is what you need for
creativity.
Six willingness attitudes

blocks.caption:
Willing to be creative, fail, be
wrong, see other views, iterate, and love problems.

blocks.html:
Attitude What it means
1. Willingness to be creative Wanting to be creative. When a problem appears, be the first to raise your hand. Don’t say, “Just tell me how to do it.”
2. Willingness to fail Creativity is not an exam. You might choose the wrong problem, the wrong idea, or implement badly. That’s okay. Not every creative effort ends in success.
3. Willingness to be wrong “I tried it, but I was wrong. What’s your view?” Then pick up the better view.
4. Willingness to see other perspectives Comes naturally once you accept you might be wrong.
5. Willingness to iterate Go back and forth between steps. If ideas don’t come, go back and redefine the problem. If you can’t implement, go back to your ideas. The steps are not a one-way road.
6. Willingness to fall in love with problems Care for the problem, don’t just tolerate it.

Take inspiration
from three creative people

blocks.caption:
A painter’s easel, a march for
freedom, and a letter that changed a life.

blocks.html:
Person What we learn
Vincent van Gogh (Dutch painter) Encouraged by his brother Theo, he painted from morning to night. He sold almost nothing in his lifetime and lived on his brother’s support, but kept painting anyway: famous works like the Sunflowers series. Today his paintings are worth a fortune. Lesson: passion, not money, drove his creativity. Read Lust for Life (a novel about his life by Irving Stone).
Mahatma Gandhi Creativity everywhere: the idea of satyagraha, the Salt March, even his simple clothes and the way he spoke. He used creativity to bring people behind a purpose.
Srinivasa Ramanujan A clerk at the Madras Port Trust, poor, but doing maths all the time and organising it neatly. He wrote a famous letter to the English professor G. H. Hardy: “Dear Sir, I beg to introduce myself to you as a clerk in the Accounts Department of the Port Trust Office at Madras…” He pointed to his best result in a way that made Hardy want to read the papers. Hardy brought him to England. Lesson: do such good work that it speaks for you.

The most
important line: creativity is deliberate

blocks.html: Creativity is a deliberate activity.
blocks.text: Creativity is a deliberate activity.

blocks.html: Deliberate means on purpose. Creativity is not an idea that suddenly falls on your head. It is solving a problem with dedication, discipline and deliberateness.

What creativity is, the journey, the
process, the tools and the attitudes.

blocks.text: What is creativity?

blocks.html:
• Everyone is creative. We only differ in our score (4/10 vs 7/10), and practice raises it.
  • Definition: bringing into existence something that did not exist before. Personal creativity counts.
  • Maslow’s needs: physiological → safety → belongingness and love → esteem → self-actualisation. We need creativity at every level.
  • Anchoring: the first (high) price you see sets your expectations.

The creativity journey

blocks.html:
• Problem → solution; it never ends. You must find and implement a solution.
  • Closure = the problem is fully solved. Most solutions are copied from others or come from experience; copying nature is biomimicry.
  • Creativity is a choice. Fall in love with problems.
  • Find problems through: the 17 UN SDGs, or empathy (the empathy walk: the mother in the hospital queue).

Process of creativity (7
steps)

blocks.html:
1. Define the problem.
  2. Collect information.
  3. Redefine the problem (hunger → adding nutrients to food).
  4. Generate ideas.
  5. Design the solution.
  6. Evaluate feasibility and refine.
  7. Implement.
blocks.text:
Define the problem. Collect information. Redefine the problem (hunger → adding nutrients to
food). Generate ideas. Design the solution. Evaluate feasibility and refine. Implement.

blocks.html:
• IDEO shopping cart: information, collaboration, ideas, prototype.
  • Worked example: “children learn English” → “fall in love with English” → summer course in England.
  • There is no guarantee of success.
